meta.title: Web Crawler
meta.summary: Crawl about a billion pages a month politely: a URL frontier with per-host politeness and priority, cached robots.txt and DNS, URL and content dedup, and adaptive recrawls.

functional: Crawl pages starting from seed URLs and from links found in fetched pages
Obey robots.txt and never send a host more than one request at a time, with a delay between requests
Store the raw HTML of every fetched page, plus metadata (status, content hash, fetch time, next crawl time)
Skip URLs that were already seen and pages whose content duplicates a page already stored
Recrawl known pages on a schedule that follows how often each one changes
nonFunctional: Sustain 1B fetched pages per month, scaling out by adding fetchers rather than through one coordinator
Politeness: one connection per host, at least 1 s (or the robots.txt Crawl-delay) between requests
Robust to crawler traps, malformed HTML and slow, broken or hostile servers
A stored raw page is never lost; a crashed component loses at most in-flight fetches, which are retried
95% of high-priority pages are recrawled within 24 hours of their due time

scale.label: Fetch rate
scale.value: 1B pages / month ≈ 400 pages/s avg, plan for ~1,000/s peak

scale.label: Bandwidth
scale.value: ~100 KB avg page ≈ 40 MB/s (~320 Mbit/s) avg, ~1 Gbit/s peak

scale.label: Raw storage
scale.value: ~25 KB per page gzipped ≈ 25 TB / month, ~300 TB / year

scale.label: URL seen set
scale.value: Bloom filter at 1% false positives ≈ 9.6 bits/URL ≈ 12 GB for 10B URLs (exact 8-byte fingerprints: 80 GB+)

scale.label: Link discovery
scale.value: ~50 links / page ≈ 20,000 URLs/s to normalize and dedup

scale.label: Hosts in flight
scale.value: 1,000 pages/s with each host fetched at most every ~2 s needs ≥ 2,000 hosts ready at once

slos.name: Crawler-side fetch success
slos.sli: Fetch attempts that did not fail because of our own components (resolver, frontier, stores, stream), divided by all fetch attempts, measured at the fetchers. Errors returned by remote sites do not count against it.

slos.name: Priority page freshness
slos.sli: High-priority pages fetched within the threshold of their next_crawl_at, divided by all high-priority pages that came due, measured from the metadata store

slos.name: Politeness
slos.sli: Requests that respected robots.txt, one connection per host and the host's delay, divided by all requests, audited from the fetchers' request log

alerts.when: Any host receives two concurrent requests or requests closer together than its delay, more than 10 times in 5 minutes
alerts.why: Hammering a site gets the crawler's IPs blocked and draws abuse complaints. It usually means two frontier shards think they own the same host, so it needs a human now.

alerts.when: Crawler-side fetch errors burning the error budget 10 times too fast over 1 hour and over 5 minutes (a slow burn, 3 times over 6 hours, opens a ticket)
alerts.why: Our own components are failing fetches, so the crawl is falling behind for every host at once.

alerts.when: More than 10% of high-priority pages that came due in the last 6 hours are still unfetched
alerts.why: The pages that matter most are going stale for whoever consumes the crawl. Usually the frontier or the scheduler is stuck.

alerts.when: Resolver cache hit ratio below 90% or p99 lookup time above 200 ms for 30 minutes
alerts.why: Slow lookups hold fetch connections idle and cut throughput. A cause to fix before freshness suffers.

alerts.when: Parser consumer lag above 30 minutes for 30 minutes
alerts.why: Fetching continues, but new links and metadata arrive late. The stream absorbs the backlog while parsers are scaled out.

alerts.when: Estimated Bloom filter false positive rate above 2%
alerts.why: Each false positive is a new URL that is silently never crawled. Rebuild the filter larger from the metadata store before coverage drops.

alerts.when: More than 100 events written to the parser dead-letter prefix in an hour
alerts.why: Pages that crash the parser are skipped, so their links and metadata are missing. Usually a parser bug or a new kind of malformed HTML.

alerts.when: A frontier shard failed to renew its ownership lease, or a shard has had no owner for 5 minutes
alerts.why: Its hosts are not being crawled at all until a new owner takes over, which freshness will show only hours later.

signals.name: Hosts ready in the politeness heap
signals.why: Fetchers can only work on hosts whose delay has passed. If this falls below the number of fetch slots, fetchers sit idle even with billions of URLs queued.

signals.name: Response code mix and fetch time per host
signals.why: A rise in 429 or 503 means we are too aggressive somewhere; fetch time feeds the per-host delay.

signals.name: Cache hit ratio and upstream lookup time
signals.why: Uncached recursive lookups take 10 to 200 ms and are the classic hidden bottleneck of a crawler.

signals.name: Filter fill ratio and estimated false positive rate
signals.why: The false positive rate rises sharply as the filter fills, so it must be resized before it is half full.

signals.name: Exact and near-duplicate share
signals.why: A sudden jump usually means a site serving one page under endless URLs: a trap the URL filters missed.

debug.symptom: Pages per second dropped, but fetchers report low CPU and few open connections
steps: Check hosts ready in the frontier heap. Few ready hosts means the frontier is dominated by a handful of large hosts all waiting out their delay.
If so, check front queue selection: discovery may have flooded the queues with one site's URLs. Cap per-host queue length and refill back queues from other hosts.
Check resolver lookup time. A cold or overloaded DNS cache makes each fetch wait before it connects.
Check robots.txt cache misses and robots fetch errors. Hosts whose robots.txt returns 5xx are treated as fully disallowed and drop out of the ready set.
Check parser lag. If parsers are behind, no new URLs reach the frontier and it slowly runs dry.

debug.symptom: A site owner reports that the crawler is overloading their server
steps: Pull the request log for the host and confirm the gaps between requests and the number of concurrent connections.
Check which frontier shard owns the host. A shard rebalance that left two owners breaks the one-connection rule.
Check whether many hostnames on the site resolve to the same IP. Politeness keyed only by hostname lets wildcard subdomains share one server; key the delay by IP or registered domain too.
Check that the robots.txt cache picked up their latest rules, and lower the TTL or purge the entry if they just changed it.

nodes.label: URL Frontier
nodes.description: Priority front queues, per-host back queues and a politeness heap; sharded by host hash. Each shard holds an ownership lease in the queue store, and fetchers and parsers address shards directly (no load balancer: the host decides the shard)

nodes.label: Caching DNS Resolver
nodes.description: Self-run resolver fleet (for example Unbound) inside the VPC; caches answers for their TTL and recurses to authoritative servers through the NAT gateways

nodes.label: Frontier Queue Store
nodes.description: Durable per-host URL queues and host state (next allowed time, backoff)

nodes.label: Robots.txt Cache
nodes.description: Parsed robots.txt rules per host, 24 h TTL

nodes.label: Content Fingerprints
nodes.description: SHA-256 of each body (global), plus 64-bit SimHash split into four 16-bit block tables keyed by registered domain

nodes.label: URL Seen Filter
nodes.description: Bloom filter bitmaps sharded by URL hash, checked and set atomically

nodes.label: Raw Page Store
nodes.description: Compressed HTML and response headers (WARC records)

nodes.label: Page Metadata DB
nodes.description: One row per known URL: status, hash, ETag, last fetch, change rate, next_crawl_at

nodes.label: Recrawl Scheduler
nodes.description: Finds known pages that are due and feeds them back to the frontier

nodes.label: Fetcher Fleet
nodes.description: Async HTTP clients, hundreds of connections each, one per host

nodes.label: Fetched Pages Stream
nodes.description: One event per fetch result, partitioned by host (politeness caps any host at about one event a second, so no partition runs hot)

nodes.label: Parser & Link Extractor
nodes.description: Extracts and normalizes links, filters traps, records metadata

nodes.label: Websites
nodes.description: Millions of independent hosts, some slow, broken or hostile

flows.title: Fetch a page (robots.txt not cached)
flows.summary: The main loop: lease a URL whose host is ready, resolve it, check robots.txt, download, dedup the content, store it and hand it to the parsers.

steps.label: POST /lease
steps.detail: Fetchers pull work instead of having it pushed, so a fetcher only takes a URL when it has a free connection slot. Each fetcher leases from the frontier shard that owns a set of hosts.

steps.label: pop politeness heap
steps.detail: Mercator design: front queues hold URLs by priority, and back queues each hold URLs for exactly one host. A min-heap keyed by each host's next allowed time gives the host that may be contacted soonest, and its back queue gives the URL. Because a host lives on one shard and one back queue, politeness needs no distributed locks.

steps.label: lease 60 s
steps.detail: The host is marked busy until the fetcher reports back or the lease expires, so no other fetcher can open a second connection to it. The fetcher cuts every request timeout to the lease time left, so it has stopped talking to the host before the lease can be re-granted, and the lease id fences /complete: a late report with an old lease id is ignored.

steps.label: A? example.org
steps.detail: Every fetch needs an IP, and an uncached recursive lookup costs 10 to 200 ms. A crawler touching millions of hosts overwhelms shared or provider resolvers, so it runs its own caching resolver fleet next to the fetchers.

steps.label: cache hit
steps.detail: Answered from cache for the record's TTL. The frontier can also prefetch DNS for hosts about to become ready, so lookups rarely sit on the fetch path.

steps.label: reject private IPs
steps.detail: URLs come from untrusted pages, so a link to an internal name could make the crawler fetch its own network or the cloud metadata endpoint. Refuse private, loopback and link-local addresses, and connect to the IP that was checked so a second lookup cannot swap it.

steps.label: GET robots:example.org
steps.detail: robots.txt applies per host and changes rarely, so the parsed rules are cached instead of being fetched before every page.

steps.label: MISS (expired)
steps.detail: The cached copy passed its 24 hour TTL, the longest RFC 9309 recommends keeping one.

steps.label: GET /robots.txt
steps.detail: Fetched over the same connection that will fetch the page. It counts toward the host's politeness budget like any other request.
steps.payload:
GET /robots.txt HTTP/1.1
Host: example.org
User-Agent: ExampleBot/2.1 (+https://crawler.example.com/bot)

steps.label: 200 text/plain
steps.detail: A 4xx means no rules (everything allowed). A 5xx or a timeout means assume everything is disallowed and try again later, because the site may be struggling.
steps.payload:
User-agent: *
Disallow: /admin/
Disallow: /search
Crawl-delay: 2
Sitemap: https://example.org/sitemap.xml

steps.label: SET EX 86400
steps.detail: Store the parsed rules, not the raw file, so every later check is a lookup. The Crawl-delay is also reported to the frontier with the result.

steps.label: /blog/post-42 allowed
steps.detail: Longest matching rule wins. A disallowed URL is dropped and recorded as blocked, without any request to the page.

steps.label: GET /blog/post-42
steps.detail: Because robots.txt was just fetched over this connection, the fetcher first waits out the host's delay (the 2 s Crawl-delay here), so the robots request also obeys politeness. One connection per host, with a 30 s total timeout (cut to the lease time left) and a 10 MB body cap so a slow or endless response cannot tie up a slot.
steps.payload:
GET /blog/post-42 HTTP/1.1
Host: example.org
User-Agent: ExampleBot/2.1 (+https://crawler.example.com/bot)
Accept: text/html
Accept-Encoding: gzip, br

steps.label: 200 text/html, 84 KB
steps.detail: The fetch took 0.4 s. That time feeds the host's delay: slower servers get proportionally more time between requests.
steps.payload:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Content-Encoding: gzip
ETag: "5f2a-61c"
Last-Modified: Mon, 09 Nov 2026 18:02:11 GMT

steps.label: SHA-256 + 64-bit SimHash
steps.detail: The exact hash catches byte-identical copies (mirrors, the same page under several URLs). SimHash, computed over the visible text, catches near-duplicates that differ only in ads, dates or session tokens.

steps.label: lookup + conditional put
steps.detail: Check the exact hash globally, then the four 16-bit SimHash blocks within the same registered domain. Two fingerprints within 3 bits must share at least one block exactly, so four keyed lookups find every near-duplicate candidate. Scoping by domain keeps each bucket small: a 16-bit key over billions of pages globally would return hundreds of thousands of candidates, which is why web-scale near-dup search uses more tables with longer keys. If the exact hash is already recorded for this same URL (an unchanged recrawl, or a retry after a crash before the page was stored), the page is stored again under the same key, which is idempotent, so a crash between these steps cannot lose it.
steps.payload:
PutItem sha256=9c1e…b7 url=https://example.org/blog/post-42
ConditionExpression: attribute_not_exists(sha256) OR url = :this_url
Query simhash_b0  pk='example.org#8f3a' (and b1, b2, b3)

steps.label: new content
steps.detail: No match, so the page is stored. A duplicate would skip storage and parsing, and only record which URL it duplicates.

steps.label: PUT raw page
steps.detail: Raw HTML goes to object storage because it is large, written once and read rarely. Keeping it means parsers can be rerun later without refetching from the site.

steps.label: 200 OK
steps.detail: Durable once acknowledged. Only now is it safe to announce the page.

steps.label: publish page_fetched
steps.detail: Parsing is CPU-bound and fetching is network-bound, so they scale separately. The event carries a pointer to the stored page, not the HTML, and the trace id from the lease, so one URL can be followed from lease to metadata write.

steps.label: POST /complete
steps.detail: Releasing the lease tells the frontier when the host may be contacted again: now plus the larger of the Crawl-delay and 10 times the last fetch time (Mercator's rule).

steps.label: ok, next at +4 s
steps.detail: The host goes back into the heap with next allowed time now + 4 s, and the slot is free for whichever host is ready next.

flows.title: Parse and discover links
flows.summary: A parser turns a fetched page into new URLs: extract, normalize, filter traps, drop ones already seen, enqueue the rest with a priority and record the page's metadata.

steps.label: deliver page_fetched
steps.detail: The stream buffers results so a slow parser fleet never slows fetching. Delivery is at least once, so every write after this must be safe to repeat.

steps.label: GET raw page
steps.detail: The event only points at the page, keeping stream messages small. The read is by key, so it is fast and cheap.

steps.label: 63 links found
steps.detail: Parse leniently (real HTML is often malformed), resolve relative links against the base URL, and respect rel=nofollow and meta robots. Links from sitemaps are added the same way.

steps.label: normalize, drop 5 traps
steps.detail: Lowercase the scheme and host, drop the fragment and default port, strip session and tracking parameters, so one page does not appear under many URLs. Reject URLs over 2,000 characters, with repeating path segments, or beyond a per-host page budget: the usual signs of a trap such as an endless calendar.

steps.label: check 58 URLs (read only)
steps.detail: About 50 links per page means 20,000 lookups a second, most for URLs already known. A Bloom filter answers in memory at about 9.6 bits per URL. URLs are grouped by shard (each URL's 7 bits live on the shard chosen by its hash) and checked with one call per shard; nothing is set yet.
steps.payload: EVALSHA bf_check 1 bf:{shard-41} <7 bit positions for each of this shard's URLs>

steps.label: 21 new, 37 seen
steps.detail: A Bloom filter has no false negatives, so a URL is never crawled twice because of it. A false positive (about 1%) makes a new URL look seen, and that URL is skipped: a small loss of coverage, accepted for the memory saved.

steps.label: enqueue 21 URLs
steps.detail: Each URL is sent to the frontier shard that owns its host, with a priority from signals such as the linking page's importance, link depth and the host's quality. The parser waits for the shard to confirm the URLs are stored.

steps.label: front queue by priority
steps.detail: New URLs land in one of a few priority front queues. Back queues refill from them, choosing high priority more often, so important pages go first without starving the rest.

steps.label: append to queues
steps.detail: Billions of queued URLs do not fit in memory. The frontier keeps only the head and tail of each queue in memory and persists the rest, so a restarted shard loses nothing. Each entry's key is derived from the URL, so enqueuing the same URL again overwrites it instead of adding a duplicate.
steps.payload: PutItem pk='example.org' sk='p2#<hash of https://example.org/blog/post-43>' depth=3

steps.label: set bits for 21 URLs
steps.detail: Bits are set only after the frontier has stored the URLs. Setting them first would lose the URLs if the parser crashed in between: the replay would find them already seen and drop them. In this order a replay simply enqueues them again, which the URL-derived keys make harmless.
steps.payload: EVALSHA bf_set 1 bf:{shard-41} <7 bit positions for each new URL on this shard>

steps.label: UpdateItem page row
steps.detail: The metadata row is the source of truth for what the crawler knows about a URL. The update is keyed by URL and overwrites fields, so a redelivered event writes the same values again.
steps.payload:
UpdateItem url=https://example.org/blog/post-42
SET status=200, sha256='9c1e…b7', etag='5f2a-61c', last_fetch=1762790400, next_crawl_at=1763395200

steps.label: commit offset
steps.detail: The offset is committed only after every write succeeded. A parser crash before this replays the event, which is safe because each write is idempotent. An event that fails 3 times (a page that crashes the parser) is written to a dead-letter prefix in the Raw Page Store and its offset committed, so one poison page cannot stall its partition.

flows.title: Recrawl a known page (304 Not Modified)
flows.summary: The scheduler feeds due pages back to the frontier. A conditional GET finds the page unchanged, so its recrawl interval grows.

steps.label: query due bucket
steps.detail: Rows are indexed by the hour they fall due, spread over many shards, so the scheduler reads only pages that are due instead of scanning 10B rows.

steps.label: 12,400 rows with ETags
steps.detail: Each row carries the stored ETag and Last-Modified, so the fetch can be conditional.

steps.label: assign priority
steps.detail: Pages that change often and matter most (home pages, news) get high priority; long-stable pages get low priority.

steps.label: enqueue 12,400
steps.detail: Recrawls go through the same frontier as new URLs, so they obey the same per-host politeness. The URL seen filter is skipped because these URLs are known on purpose.

steps.label: 202 accepted
steps.detail: The scheduler moves each row to a pending state so the next run does not enqueue it again. Pending rows whose fetch never reported back within a day are picked up again, so a URL dropped by a parked host is retried rather than forgotten.

steps.label: POST /lease
steps.detail: Later, when the host's turn comes, a fetcher leases the URL like any other.

steps.label: GET If-None-Match
steps.detail: DNS and robots.txt come from cache as in the main flow (not shown). A conditional request lets the server skip sending the body when nothing changed.
steps.payload:
GET /about HTTP/1.1
Host: example.org
If-None-Match: "77b-5d0"
If-Modified-Since: Tue, 03 Nov 2026 09:00:00 GMT

steps.label: 304 Not Modified
steps.detail: No body, so bandwidth and storage are saved. Servers that ignore these headers return 200, and the content hash then shows whether anything changed.

steps.label: POST /complete
steps.detail: Releases the host so its delay starts counting.

steps.label: publish not_modified
steps.detail: The same stream carries every fetch outcome, so metadata is always written in one place.

steps.label: interval × 2 (max 30 d)
steps.detail: Adaptive recrawl: an unchanged page waits twice as long next time, and a changed one waits half as long (down to an hour). Crawl budget flows to pages that actually change.

steps.label: UpdateItem next_crawl_at
steps.payload:
UpdateItem url=https://example.org/about
SET last_fetch=1762790400, interval_h=192, next_crawl_at=1763481600

flows.title: Host slow or failing (backoff)
flows.summary: A host answers 503. The frontier backs that host off exponentially while fetchers keep working on other hosts.

steps.label: GET /p/1187
steps.detail: DNS and robots.txt come from cache (not shown). The site is overloaded and takes 8 s to answer.

steps.label: classify: retryable
steps.detail: Timeouts, connection resets, 429 and 5xx are retryable and say the host is struggling. 404 and 410 are permanent: the URL is marked gone and not retried.

steps.label: POST /complete status=503
steps.detail: The fetcher reports the outcome instead of retrying itself, because only the frontier knows the host's schedule.

steps.label: host waits ≥ 120 s
steps.detail: The whole host backs off, not just the URL: next allowed time = now + max(Retry-After, 60 s × 2^failures) with jitter, capped at 24 h. The URL goes back on its host queue with attempt 2. After 5 consecutive failures the host is parked for a day and its URLs are recorded as failed.

steps.label: save host backoff
steps.detail: Backoff state is durable so a frontier restart does not immediately hit a struggling site again.

steps.label: POST /lease
steps.detail: The fetcher immediately asks for more work: its slot is free.

steps.label: heap top: another host
steps.detail: The failing host now sits deep in the heap. Because each host has its own back queue, one bad site cannot block URLs from any other site.

notes.text: Mercator-style frontier: a few priority front queues decide what is important, and back queues (about 3 per fetch slot, one host each) plus a heap of next allowed times enforce politeness. Sharding by host hash keeps all of a host's state on one node, so politeness needs no per-request coordination. A shard serves its hosts only while it holds an ownership lease in the queue store; on a rebalance the new owner waits until the old lease and the longest fetch lease have run out, so two shards never lease the same host.

A Bloom filter for 10B URLs at 1% false positives takes about 12 GB, against 80 GB or more for exact 8-byte fingerprints. False positives mean some new URLs are never crawled; nothing is crawled twice. The metadata store keeps the exact list, so the filter can be rebuilt larger when it fills (an offline job, not drawn). Losing recent bits in a cache failover only causes some URLs to be enqueued twice, which the frontier's URL-derived keys absorb.

DNS is a classic crawler bottleneck: lookups are slow, standard resolver libraries block a thread, and managed resolvers throttle per-interface query rates. A self-run caching resolver with async lookups and prefetch for hosts about to be fetched keeps it off the critical path.

About 25 TB a month of compressed HTML. One object per page means a billion PUT requests a month; appending pages into ~1 GB WARC files and storing offsets cuts request cost by orders of magnitude, at the cost of buffering on the fetcher. Older crawls move to colder storage classes.

Fetchers follow URLs written by strangers. Block private, loopback and link-local addresses after resolving (and connect to the checked IP) to prevent server-side request forgery, cap body size and time, and never execute fetched content. Identify the bot with a User-Agent and contact URL, and send traffic from fixed NAT IPs that site owners can verify.

Websites are the least reliable part of the system: slow responses, 5xx, robots.txt outages and traps that generate infinite URLs. Per-host backoff, per-host page budgets and URL length and depth limits keep one bad site from consuming the crawl.

questions.q: How do you crawl 1,000 pages a second without overloading any single website?
questions.a: Give every host its own back queue in the frontier and a next allowed time, kept in a min-heap, so a host is leased to only one fetcher at a time and only after its delay has passed. The delay is the larger of the robots.txt Crawl-delay and about 10 times the last fetch time, so slow servers get more breathing room. Throughput comes from crawling thousands of hosts in parallel, not from crawling one host faster.

questions.q: Why use a Bloom filter for the URL seen set, and what happens on a false positive?
questions.a: With 10B URLs an exact set of fingerprints needs 80 GB or more, while a Bloom filter at 1% false positives needs about 12 GB and answers in memory. It never gives false negatives, so no URL is crawled twice because of it. A false positive makes a new URL look seen, so it is skipped and never crawled: a small loss of coverage traded for memory, which you size the filter to keep low.

questions.q: Many URLs serve the same or almost the same content. How do you avoid storing and parsing it again?
questions.a: Hash the body for exact duplicates and compute a 64-bit SimHash of the visible text for near-duplicates, where pages within about 3 bits are treated as the same. To find matches without scanning, split the SimHash into four 16-bit blocks and index each, here within a registered domain: two fingerprints within 3 bits must share at least one block exactly. Across the whole web a 16-bit key matches far too many pages, so global near-dup detection uses more tables keyed on longer bit groups. A duplicate is recorded against the original URL but not stored or parsed again.

questions.q: How do you stop the crawler from getting stuck in a trap such as an infinite calendar?
questions.a: Normalize URLs so session IDs and tracking parameters do not create endless variants, and reject URLs that are too long, too deep or repeat path segments. Give each host a page budget per crawl cycle, so even an undetected trap can only consume that host's share. A sudden rise in near-duplicate pages from one host is a good signal that a trap got through.

questions.q: How do you decide when to recrawl a page you have already fetched?
questions.a: Estimate each page's change rate from history: if a recrawl finds it unchanged (a 304 or the same content hash), double its interval, and if it changed, halve it, within bounds such as one hour to 30 days. Store next_crawl_at in the metadata store, indexed by due time, so the scheduler reads only due pages. Use conditional GETs with the stored ETag so unchanged pages cost almost no bandwidth.

questions.q: A fetcher crashes in the middle of a fetch. What happens to that URL, and can a page be processed twice?
questions.a: The frontier leased the URL with a timeout, so when the lease expires the URL goes back on its host's queue and is fetched again; nothing is lost, and the old fetcher's late report is ignored because its lease id is stale. Processing is at least once: the same page can be fetched or delivered to a parser twice. That is safe because the content store write is conditional (a repeat from the same URL is idempotent), metadata updates are keyed by URL, frontier entries are keyed by URL, and the parser marks URLs seen only after the frontier has stored them.
